terms.gloss: more of a thing you measure: more food, more time, more milk
terms.grammar: neuter noun, used in the nominative and accusative, with the thing in the genitive
evidence: Cic. Sen. 66: eō plūs viāticī quaerere
terms.comment: In the singular “more” is a noun, “a greater amount”, and what there is more of goes into the genitive: plūs cibī, more food; plūs temporis, more time; plūs lactis, more milk. On its own it is simply “more”: plūs volō, I want more. “Much more” is multō plūs; “more than enough”, plūs satis; “less” works the same way, minus labōris.

terms.gloss: more of things you count: more balls, more books
terms.grammar: adjective, plural, agreeing with its noun; genitive plūrium
evidence: Plin. Ep. 8.16.5: plūra fortasse quam dēbuī; sed pauciōra quam voluī
terms.comment: In the plural “more” is an adjective and agrees: plūrēs pilae, more balls; plūrēs librōs, more books; plūra, more things. So “give me more milk” is plūs lactis, but “give me more books” is plūrēs librōs. The singular with a genitive plural is classical too (plūs voluptātum, Cic. Fin. 1.62), but plūrēs is the everyday way. “Fewer” is pauciōrēs, never minus with a plural.

terms.gloss: more, further, any more: something added to what there already is
terms.grammar: adverb, and a neuter used as a noun
terms.comment: “More” in the sense of “further, in addition”: Vīs amplius?, would you like some more?; nihil amplius, nothing more. With a number, amplius and plūs mean “more than” and may drop quam without changing the case: amplius ducentōs, more than two hundred.

terms.gloss: again, once more: more of doing something
terms.comment: “More!” when what is wanted is the action again, not a larger amount: Lege etiam!, read some more; etiam atque etiam, again and again. With a plain statement etiam is “also, even”, so volō etiam is “I want it too”; “I want more” is plūs volō, and “even more”, etiam plūs.

phrases.english: can anything be sillier than to look for more provisions the less road is left?
